newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania creates special police to take on gunmen.
newsitem.headline: Albania creates special police to take on gunmen.

text.p: The Albanian government has set up special police units to confront and disarm gunmen who have brought the country to anarchy, paying them up to 30 times the average wage, Justice Minister Spartak Ngjela said on Saturday.

The new minister also said he was ready to go to the south of the country to negotiate with anti-government rebels who have taken control of most of the region and are demanding the resignation of President Sali Berisha.

Ngjela, appointed only on Thursday as part of an all-party government to tackle the crisis, said a handful of special units were operating initially in the capital, receiving between $50 and $100 a day for the dangerous work.
This compares to the average wage of $70 to $100 a month in Albania, Europe's poorest country.
The move is clearly aimed at tackling the lawlessness ripping the country apart after civilians looted barracks as the army disintegrated and nervous police melted away.
It follows another decision by the minister, announced on Friday, to increase police pay by 300 percent and to bring the hated secret police under control of the government rather than the president.
Since Friday a police armoured car with new recruits firing in the air has been driving around the capital in a highly visible attempt to show the population that order was being restored.
"Foreign governments have agreed to help us resolve this crisis, but only on condition that order is restored," he said.

The moves appeared to have had an effect as Tirana experienced its quietest night for several. The minister said the new units had already succeeded in disarming some gunmen, though he had no exact figures.
At Tirana's main police station Number Two, a crowd of some 200 people were waiting outside to join up to the new units.
"I am for peace and calm, and if I'm called I am ready," said Gazim, waiting in line.
But he warned: "You have to select people. Not all are good. Some people want to take advantage of this situation."

New Albanian Prime Minister Bashkim Fino said on Friday he had discussed with European mediator Franz Vranitzky the possible creation of an international police force to help restore order, particularly in disarming the gunmen.
But he expressed the hope that Albanians would be able to do this themselves and such a force would not be needed.

Ngjela, who spent 17 years in jail for opposition to Stalinist leader Enver Hoxha and was the last political prisoner to be released, in 1991, said his main priority was to restore order in Tirana, in northern Albania.
"The situation in all the north is very bad, but our first priority was to tackle Tirana," he said.

Most towns in the north are reported to under the rule of the gun, particularly the port of Durres 30 km (20 miles) west of Tirana, where armed violence hampered the evacuation of foreign nationals by sea on Thursday.

Ngjela said the situation in the south, which rose in anger over collapsed pyramid savings schemes for which local people blamed the president and the government, was different, with a measure of control administered by self-governing rebel councils.
The minister said he was ready to go to Vlore, the focus of the southern revolt, to negotiate with the rebels.
He said the idea was for a stage-by-stage process, with the government initially negotiating with individual rebel councils on their gradual reintegration into state structures.
